beats.narration_text: Ciao, this is Liam, in for Bear. Jow-hway Lee's Dusk Duel is a 2D fighting game. Assignment five adds two shaders Jow-hway typed by hand: a red flash on whichever fighter was just hit, and a granite surface in the 3D prop room. Claude wrote the driver, the tests and the audit. This film follows what the tests proved, and what only eyes could judge.

beats.narration_text: So what is a shader? A small program the graphics card runs for every pixel of this sprite, all at once. Line one makes it a canvas item shader, for 2D. Lines three and four are uniforms: values the game can set. Line seven is the colour line, mixing the pixel's colour toward the flash colour.

show.event: line 3 highlights: hurt_amount: set by game code

props.title: What A Shader Does
props.source: Godot editor reconstruction · godot/shaders/hurt_flash.gdshader lines 1-8 · source 043df17 · typed by Zhaohui

beats.narration_text: Here's line seven's output, captured from the running engine with the value set from code. Every sampled pixel lands within one step of Jow-hway's arithmetic. The steady one-step shortfall is the sprite's alpha: two fifty-four, not two fifty-five.

show.event: three captures with sample rings; 0.0 card lights

props.title: Within One Step
props.status: OBSERVED · tests/capture_a5.gd · in-engine capture, driver paused

beats.narration_text: A shader remembers nothing, so game state has to arrive as a uniform. This driver is Claude's. Lines nineteen to twenty-one give each fighter its own material: the material holds the values, the shader is shared. Line twenty-seven reads the stun counter once per physics tick, so the flash lasts twenty-two ticks at any frame rate.

show.event: line 18 highlights: runs after the fight steps
line 19 highlights: a new material per fighter
line 21 highlights: set on this sprite only
line 27 highlights: the value from game state

props.title: Material Holds The Value
props.source: Godot editor reconstruction · godot/fighter/hurt_flash.gd lines 15-28 · source 043df17 · written by Claude
props.code:
func _ready() -> void:
	# main.gd steps the fighters at the default priority 0; a higher value runs after it, so the
	# value set here is the one for the state of this same tick.
	process_physics_priority = 100
	material = ShaderMaterial.new()
	material.shader = SHADER
	sprite.material = material


func _physics_process(_delta: float) -> void:
	var amount := 0.0
	if fighter.state == "hurt":
		amount = float(fighter.stun) / float(Fighter.HITSTUN)
	material.set_shader_parameter("hurt_amount", amount)

beats.narration_text: That's why, when Ah-oh-tah-keh's kick lands, only Ah-kah-ken flashes. One shader, two materials, two separate flash values.

beats.narration_text: Jow-hway predicted that hint range would not clamp a value set from code. With the red flash you can't tell: one and two both saturate. With grey, two gives thirty-four, one sixty-seven: the mix, extrapolated. Not clamped. The prediction held.

beats.narration_text: The headless test drives the real game loop with the J key and samples the value every frame, at thirty, sixty and a hundred and forty-four frames per second. Its first run failed four checks: a second hit can't land during hurt in real play, and time scale doesn't slow the fight. Jow-hway revised the brief, not the assertions. Now sixty-nine pass at every rate.

show.event: first run and revised run side by side; Loop card lights

props.title: Revise The Brief, Not The Test

beats.narration_text: Then Jow-hway broke the shaders on purpose. A missing semicolon: the uniform list comes back empty. A renamed uniform still parses, and all twenty-three behaviour checks still pass, because setting a name the shader doesn't have raises no error. Only the uniform list noticed. Deleting source colour fails the material test.

show.event: three mutations with what caught each; Semicolon card lights

props.title: Break It On Purpose
props.status: HEADLESS · each mutation made by Zhaohui, then restored

beats.narration_text: Now a texture. Why is it information, not a picture? Lines three to five are three files of numbers. Line three says source colour: these numbers are colour, so they get decoded first. Line four has no such hint: roughness, read as stored. Line five marks a normal map. The uniforms below are Inspector controls, in two groups.

show.event: line 3 highlights: albedo: read as colour
line 4 highlights: roughness: read as data

props.title: A Texture Is Numbers
props.source: Godot editor reconstruction · godot/shaders/granite.gdshader lines 1-23 · source 043df17 · typed by Zhaohui

beats.narration_text: Two materials share that shader: the floor at U V scale six, the plinth at one, tinted the A3 stone colour. Change one value in one material, and only the floor changes. Edit one shader line, Jow-hway checked, and both change. And Jow-hway's verdict on the granite: it looks like wooden planks. The box U Vs stretch it.

beats.narration_text: Each uniform swept to its ends. U V scale changes the grain; roughness and normal strength change how the light sits on it; and tint at black, Jow-hway said, isn't good-looking.

beats.narration_text: The hint experiment asks what a hint does to the number the shader receives. One three-pixel file: greys sixty-four, one twenty-eight and one ninety-two. Line four reads it with source colour, line five without. The true-or-false switch on line seven picks which one writes albedo, on an unshaded quad.

props.title: Same File, Two Hints
props.source: Godot editor reconstruction · godot/shaders/hint_experiment.gdshader lines 1-15 · source 043df17 · typed by Zhaohui

beats.narration_text: Jow-hway predicted quad B would brighten, to one thirty-seven, one eighty-eight and two twenty-four. Both quads show the stored values. In Godot's Compatibility renderer, every albedo is decoded, whatever the hint, then encoded on output. The prediction followed the Forward-plus pipeline. This project had to measure first.

show.event: capture beside the predicted and measured table; Predicted B card lights

props.title: Predicted 137, Measured 64
props.imageLabel: quad A above, quad B below

beats.narration_text: And what is the Godot shading language? Close to G L S L, but you pick a shader type instead of writing main, and hints shape the Inspector. Here's the shader Godot generated for a standard material, beside Jow-hway's. The albedo lines match. The normal map uses hint roughness normal, which in the editor also feeds the roughness import.

show.event: two pairs of lines; Type card lights

beats.narration_text: So what did the tests prove? That the shaders parse, that their uniforms are declared and driven, and that the materials are wired, even from an empty cache. Not how anything looks. Those are Jow-hway's checks, in Jow-hway's words: the flash can be seen, the quads are alike, the granite looks like wood. The screenshot comparison wasn't done.

show.event: proves and cannot, side by side; Proves card lights

beats.narration_text: Verdict. Checked: sixty-nine checks at three frame rates, ninety-six material checks from an empty cache, three mutations that fail, and pixels within one step of the hand predictions. Uncertain: the retrigger is reachable only by test setup, and the screenshot comparison wasn't done. Claude got four things wrong: an outdated command line tool, null material values, captures sampled at the wrong scale, and a wrong claim about hint normal. Jow-hway typed every shader line, predicted, broke and judged them; Claude wrote the driver, the tests, the audit and the captures. Next step: a U V scale per axis, so the granite stops looking like planks.
